ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial video-call style with mostly short to medium turns, though speakers give long, structured presentation segments. Early chat is informal and overlapping, full of greetings, technical checks, side conversations, laughter-like affirmations, repetitions, and fillers such as “yeah,” “um,” “okay,” and “right.” Participants hedge frequently—“I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “I guess,” “it seems”—especially when speculating, while questions are often prefaced as “quick,” “naive,” or “good” questions. Formality rises during introductions and talks, then drops again in Q&A, where people openly build on prior questions, acknowledge good points, and frame challenges as curiosity rather than contradiction. Disagreement is indirect and collaborative, typically expressed through alternatives, caveats, or admissions of uncertainty. Speakers often self-correct, restart phrases, repeat words, and use conversational signposting like “so,” “all right,” and “what I mean is,” creating an unpolished but friendly academic feel.

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, mine. I got through most of the interviews, I think fourteen of twenty, and the rest are scheduled for the following two weeks.
  - Fourteen, nice. Were those all from the first batch?
  - Most of them. A couple were referrals.
Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Choosing which retrofits to fund so older apartment buildings stay safe during multi-day heat waves.

speakers.name: Maya Chen
speakers.background: Maya is a licensed building-performance engineer with 14 years of experience diagnosing overheating in multifamily housing. She leads field studies that combine whole-building energy models, short-term indoor temperature and humidity monitoring, envelope inspections, and electrical load assessments. She has designed retrofit specifications for municipal affordable-housing programs and is accustomed to translating technical uncertainty into procurement-ready packages.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya frames the pilot as a coupled envelope-and-electricity reliability problem. She wants a technically standardized baseline package—roof insulation, exterior shading, efficient in-unit cooling, and electrical-panel upgrades where load calculations require them—so outcomes can be compared across 20 buildings. She argues that calibrated indoor-temperature modeling can rank candidates by overheating risk, but insists that panel capacity, feeder constraints, and coincident cooling demand be checked before adding air conditioning, both to prevent unsafe overloads and to avoid localized grid stress during heat events.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Romero
speakers.background: Luis is a doctoral candidate in environmental health with six years of mixed-methods research on urban heat, housing precarity, and emergency-care utilization. He has worked with hospital syndromic-surveillance data, tenant interviews, wearable and indoor environmental sensors, and community organizations serving older adults and homebound residents. His dissertation examines how heat exposure is shaped by mobility, chronic illness, and housing conditions.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Luis treats indoor heat as an exposure pathway rather than simply a building-performance failure. He would prioritize buildings serving older residents and households in areas with prior heat-related emergency visits, then evaluate the pilot using continuous indoor-temperature data alongside reported heat symptoms, sleep disruption, medication-related vulnerability, and care-seeking. He cautions that common-area cooling rooms and public cooling centers are not equivalent to in-home protection for people who cannot travel, have mobility limitations, care responsibilities, or safety concerns about leaving their apartments.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Priya Shah
speakers.background: Priya is a doctoral student in applied economics with five years of research experience in household energy demand, utility affordability, and housing-policy evaluation. Her work uses administrative utility-bill data, tenant surveys, quasi-experimental program evaluation, and distributional cost-benefit analysis. She has advised local nonprofits on energy-burden screening but has limited experience with electrical engineering and defers on equipment specifications.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya focuses on incidence: who actually pays for, can operate, and benefits from the retrofit. She sees a tenant-operated air-conditioning package as potentially ineffective if electricity costs are shifted onto low-income residents, who may ration cooling during the very heat waves the pilot is meant to address. She would require an energy-burden safeguard—such as utility-bill support or an owner-paid electricity arrangement—before treating installed cooling as protective, and would measure actual cooling use, tenant bills, arrearages, and self-reported cost-related curtailment. She can frame the safeguard as a testable pilot condition while noting that its legal and fiscal feasibility must be confirmed before the June 20 recommendation.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

meeting_opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting where one discipline dominates airtime and a quieter participant raises a substantive point that should change the plan. The evaluated AI must identify disciplines and summarize perspectives by substance, preserving the quieter contribution.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where one discipline dominates airtime and a quieter participant raises a substantive point that should change the plan. The evaluated AI must identify disciplines and summarize perspectives by substance, preserving the quieter contribution.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a planning meeting with Maya Chen (environmental engineering), Dr. Luis Romero (public health), and Priya Shah (economics). Maya should dominate the meeting, speaking for most of the time and pressing for a technically standardized package: roof insulation, exterior shading, efficient in-unit cooling, and panel upgrades where needed. She should explain that indoor-temperature modeling can rank buildings by overheating risk and that panel capacity and coincident cooling demand must be checked to avoid local grid problems. Luis should contribute a shorter but clear public-health perspective: prioritize buildings with older residents and prior heat-related emergency visits, measure indoor temperatures and heat symptoms, and recognize that cooling centers may not protect people who cannot travel or safely leave home. Priya should speak relatively little and be interrupted or passed over initially, but she must raise a substantive issue before the meeting ends: a package centered on tenant-operated air conditioning can shift electricity costs onto tenants, causing low-income residents to limit use during heat waves; therefore the pilot should not judge a retrofit as protective based only on installed equipment. Her point should change the proposed plan by requiring a tenant energy-burden safeguard, such as utility-bill support or an owner-paid electricity arrangement, and measurement of actual cooling use and bills. Keep the meeting focused on deciding what to take to the June 20 budget committee. The final recommendation may remain contingent on confirming the cost and legal feasibility of the electricity safeguard.

disciplines_and_perspectives.perspective: Use indoor-temperature modeling to identify overheated buildings and fund a standardized physical retrofit package of insulation, exterior shading, efficient in-unit cooling, and electrical upgrades as needed. Assess panel capacity and coincident cooling demand so the package does not create grid or building electrical constraints.

Target residents and buildings with elevated health vulnerability, including older adults and locations with prior heat-related emergency visits. Evaluate heat symptoms alongside indoor conditions, and do not assume cooling centers are an adequate substitute for safe in-home temperatures.

Evaluate affordability and incentive effects, especially who pays for added electricity. Tenant-operated air conditioning may be unused if residents face unaffordable bills, so installed cooling equipment alone is not evidence of protection.

dominant_airtime.evidence: Maya leads most of the discussion and advocates the initial standardized technical package.

quieter_contribution_to_preserve.substantive_point: A cooling-centered retrofit can fail during a heat wave if tenants bear electricity costs and reduce air-conditioner use because of cost.
quieter_contribution_to_preserve.required_plan_change: Add a tenant energy-burden safeguard, such as bill assistance or an owner-paid electricity arrangement, and collect data on actual cooling use and tenant bills.

decision_status.provisional_decision: Bring a targeted retrofit pilot proposal to the June 20 budget committee that combines building overheating and electrical screening with health-vulnerability targeting.
decision_status.unresolved_dependency: Confirm the cost and legal feasibility of the tenant electricity safeguard before finalizing the program design.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. Before we get into it, hope folks have survived the first really warm stretch. What I'd most like out of today is to get to a version of the pilot package that we can actually defend as comparable across all 20 buildings, and where the electrical screening isn't treated as an afterthought.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: For comparability, I’d want a minimum in-unit monitoring protocol, not just whole-building metrics. Otherwise we can show a mean- I mean, an average improvement while top-floor bedrooms and people with limited mobility remain dangerously exposed overnight.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Exactly. I'd make the unit placement stratified, at least top floor versus lower floor, shaded versus unshaded where we can, because the within-building spread can be enormous. I saw that in the walk-up we discussed. The top floor stayed hot well after the outdoor temperature fell, and a building-average model really, um, blurred that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I'd add bedroom placement specifically. In our post-event interviews, people described severe sleep disruption after three nights, even where daytime spot readings looked tolerable, so the overnight tail may be the health-relevant...

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d treat overnight bedroom temperature as a required outcome, not an optional add-on. And it changes the engineering screen a bit too. We shouldn’t assume a common cooling room substitutes for in-unit cooling if people need relief while they’re sleeping, especially on the top floor.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly—overnight exposure is where a cooling-room-only package really starts to look inadequate.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: And it means the cooling specification has to be usable at night, not just nominally installed. Before we promise in-unit units across the board, though, I need the electrical screen. The panel rating, feeder condition, and a heat-wave coincident-load estimate, because those top-floor units all running overnight are exactly where an older service can become the- where the constraint could be.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: And that screen needs to be paired with who actually needs overnight protection. I was thinking mobility, respiratory or cardiac medications, caregiving... because the electrical constraint isn't neutral if it leaves the most heat-vulnerable tenants relying on a cooling room.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'd keep the physical package standard, but let the eligibility and sequencing reflect that vulnerability screen. If a service upgrade can't happen in the pilot window, we should be explicit that a portable unit alone isn't an equivalent intervention. Luis, do you think we can collect the health information at the unit level without making recruitment too burdensome, or...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I think so, if we keep it really lean. A brief baseline vulnerability screen, then short symptom and sleep check-ins around heat events, linked to the monitor. We should also make clear that participation is voluntary and not tied to tenancy, obviously.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: That sounds workable. I'd want the monitor deployment tied to that same lean screen, so we can make sure the bedrooms we instrument include tenants for whom overnight heat is most consequential. Not- not just the easiest units for the landlord to give us access to.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: We should track who declines or can’t sustain participation too. If landlord-selected access- if the landlord is picking who we can reach, that could otherwise leave out the most isolated tenants. The brief screen can ask about mobility and caregiving without becoming invasive.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: And that affects the engineering data too. If access goes through the landlord, we may end up monitoring the simpler, better-maintained units and calibrating to the wrong part of the building. I think each landlord should give us a transparent unit-sampling list with floor, orientation, and occupancy if tenants choose to share it, and we recruit from that instead of letting access happen ad hoc.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: And we should retain a record of refusals and unavailable units by floor and orientation. Otherwise the sampling frame can look transparent on paper while the people with the highest exposure, or the least ability to participate... while they're still systematically absent.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: And from the building side, I'd add a site-access log too. If top-floor or rear units are repeatedly unavailable, that's useful context in itself, not something we quietly smooth over. We can pre-specify minimum strata for each building, then flag buildings where recruitment can't meet them instead of pretending the monitoring sample is representative, because...

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: One thing I'd put alongside that sampling protocol before June 20 is, for any in-unit AC, installation can't be our exposure measure. If the tenant bears the incremental electricity cost, they may ration it overnight, so the pilot needs a bill-support or owner-paid-electricity—I'm losing the thread. Before we call that package protective, we need a safeguard, and I'm not sure yet which structure is legally or fiscally viable.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: That has to be in the definition of a completed retrofit. A high-efficiency unit that the household cannot afford to run through the third hot night is not really a cooling intervention, and it will also make our measured results look like an equipment failure when it isn't. Priya, do you have any early sense from the bill data whether overnight rationing shows up clearly enough to measure?

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Not cleanly from consumption alone, at least not in the small sample. Similar summer kWh came with really different reported AC use, maybe because of shared meters, efficiency, schedules, or reporting. I’d pair interval bills, where available, with a very short heat-event use and cost- curtailment check-in.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: That makes sense. We should treat the check-in as part of the operating condition of the equipment, alongside the electrical screen, not try to infer it from kWh after the fact. Priya, do you think a very short nightly prompt during a declared heat event could distinguish “didn't need it” from “wanted to run it but held back because of cost,” or is that already too much burden?

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: I think it can, if it's literally two items the morning after a heat night. Whether they ran it, and if not, or less than they wanted, whether cost was the reason. We should allow a paper or phone option, though, because app-only check-ins will select people out, and...

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Paper and phone need to be built in from the start. And from my side, I'd want the prompt to capture whether the unit was physically available to run, like a tripped breaker or a shared outlet issue, because otherwise we could code non-use as cost when it was really an electrical or installation failure.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: The morning check-in should separate that from symptoms and sleep. Otherwise someone may report non-use as a technical issue, but they may have- they could still have had a really harmful overnight exposure. Those are different failure pathways.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d keep those as separate fields all the way through. Equipment availability, actual use and the reason for curtailed use, then the overnight temperature and symptom or sleep outcome. Otherwise we won’t know if a bad bedroom result points to the envelope, the panel and installation, affordability, or the unit just being undersized.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: For the health analysis, those are distinct causal pathways, not just covariates. I’d also include a morning sleep-disruption- I’d put in a morning sleep-disruption item, since it may register harm before someone seeks care.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm-hm. And because sleep disruption may be our earliest signal, the monitors need enough resolution to link that morning report to the actual overnight bedroom profile, not just a daily maximum. I think we can keep it fairly, fairly lean, with temperature and humidity at, say, 10- or 15-minute intervals, then align that to the heat-event check-in. I’d need to confirm what the procurement options support.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there and follow up by email on the remaining details. Thanks, everyone, this was really helpful.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: All right, take care, everyone.
